summary: This specification defines a TLS handshake message for exchanging supplemental application data. Hello message extensions determine which supplemental data types both client and server support, and the new message carries the data. Other documents define the specific types. It updates RFC 4346 and was later updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: When two computers set up a secure connection, they can slip in an extra envelope of useful information too. This defines the envelope and how they agree on what goes inside.

how do tls clients negotiate supplemental data
subtitle: A TLS handshake message that carries extra application data, such as authorization hints, alongside the normal handshake.

tldr.problem: Proposals kept needing to send application-specific data, such as user name hints or authorization assertions, during the TLS handshake, and defining a separate handshake message for each would multiply messages.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4680 defines one supplemental_data handshake message (type 23) that bundles all such data objects. Client and server first agree on supplemental data types using TLS hello extensions.
tldr.outcome: The message only carries data for applications above TLS. Each data type and its extension is defined in other documents, and this RFC updates RFC 4346 and has itself been updated.

today: RFC 4680 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4346. It has itself been updated by RFC 8447 and RFC 8996, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Need for Supplemental Data
sections.content:
Recent standards activity had proposed ways of sending supplemental application data in the TLS handshake. This is data that TLS itself does not process, but that helps the TLS-protected application make authentication and authorization decisions. One proposal sends user name hints for locating credentials. Another sends attribute certificates and SAML assertions for authorization checks.

To avoid defining one handshake message per kind of data, this RFC defines a single new handshake message that bundles all data objects destined for the application. It is specified in the TLS Presentation Language of RFC 2246.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a handshake where you also want to hand over a note for the person you are meeting. Instead of inventing a new kind of note every time, there is one standard envelope that can hold any of them.

sections.title: The supplemental_data Message
sections.content:
The new supplemental_data handshake message has type value 23. Its body is a SupplementalData structure holding a list of SupplementalDataEntry items (between 1 and 2^24-1 bytes). Each entry has a supp_data_type, a 16-bit supp_data_length giving the length in bytes of the data, and the data itself, whose format depends on the type.

The RFC defines no actual types: the SupplementalDataType enum is empty apart from its maximum, (65535). Other documents define specific types, their syntax and processing, and the hello extensions used to negotiate them.

Information in an entry MUST be intended exclusively for applications and protocols above TLS, and TLS MUST NOT need to process it. If the message is present it MUST contain a non-empty entry for at least one defined type.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope has a label saying what kind of note is inside, how long it is, and then the note. This RFC makes the envelope but leaves the list of note types blank for others to fill in.

sections.title: Agreeing in Advance
sections.content:
Supplemental data must never arrive as a surprise. For each SupplementalDataType, client and server MUST first reach an explicit agreement using TLS extensions in the client and server hello messages.

Each side may send at most one SupplementalData message. Receiving more than one, or receiving one that was not agreed, is a fatal error: the receiver MUST close the connection with a fatal unexpected_message alert. Data can flow client to server, server to client, or both ways.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone hands over a note, both sides say in their greetings what kinds of notes they can handle. A surprise note gets the call hung up.

sections.title: Message Flow
sections.content: If it is used, the SupplementalData message MUST be sent as the first handshake message after the hello messages, as shown in the RFC's Figure 1. The server sends it right after its ServerHello, before Certificate. The client sends it before its own Certificate. Both are marked as optional or situation-dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: The note goes first in line, right after the hellos, before the identity cards are shown.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Each supplemental data type brings its own security properties, so the document defining the type must discuss them. This RFC adds one general concern: because of where the message sits, the server provides its supplemental data before the client is authenticated, and in many cases a server will not want to share authorization information with an unauthenticated client.

The RFC's answer is the double handshake. A first handshake without extensions sets up protected communication. A second handshake, carried inside that protection and including the extensions and SupplementalData, then runs after both parties are authenticated. The messages of the second handshake are protected by both TLS sessions.
sections.plainLanguage: If the note is private, first make a safe tunnel with a plain handshake, then do the real handshake with the note inside the tunnel, so nobody outside can read it and both sides already know who they are talking to.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA added an entry supplemental_data(23) to the existing HandshakeType registry from RFC 2246. It also created a new registry for TLS Supplemental Data Formats.

In that registry, values 0 to 16385 are assigned by Standards Action, values 16386 to 65279 by IETF Consensus, and values 65280 to 65535 are reserved for Private Use, following RFC 2434.
sections.plainLanguage: A central list keeps track of the note types so two different groups do not pick the same number. Some number ranges are strict, and some are left for private use.

messages.note: Ends with Finished messages; later traffic is protected by session one.

messages.note: Second handshake, inside the first session.
